chunks: Power equations: P = VI. The question: What is the equation to find power?
Power is how fast energy is being used or turned into heat. In an electrical part, it equals voltage times current, P equals VI , measured in watts.
Knowing the power tells you how hot a part gets and how fast a battery drains.
Think of a waterfall driving a water wheel. The power depends on how far the water falls (voltage) and how much water flows each second (current).
A tall waterfall with a trickle and a short one with a huge flow can deliver the same power.
Add Ohm's law and the same power can be written using only current and resistance, or only voltage and resistance.
Power pulses at twice the source frequency. For a resistor it never goes negative and averages V pI p/2 = 10 watts.
With a 60° phase shift it dips negative (energy flows back to the source) and averages half as much. A pure reactance swings symmetrically and averages zero.
Drag φ toward 90°: the negative lobes grow until the average (red line) reaches zero, and the red curve becomes the dashed reactance case.
Power (P): energy used per second, measured in watts (W). Energy: the capacity to do work or make heat, measured in joules (J). One watt is one joule per second.
Dissipation: power turned into heat in a part. Power rating: the most power a part can safely dissipate. Ohm's law: V equals IR .
Put 12 volts across a 1 kilohms resistor. The current is 12 over 1000 equals 12 milliamps. The power is 12 times 0. 012 equals 0. 144 watts, or 144 milliwatts .
Using the resistor form gives the same answer: V squared over R equals 144 over 1000 equals 0. 144 watts.
Many small resistors are rated well below that, so this one would overheat. That is the whole idea.
"Power is P equals VI , voltage times current, which is energy per second.
For a resistor you can substitute Ohm's law to get I to the 2R or V squared over R , whichever uses what you know.
For AC, average power is V rmsI rms cosine , so a pure capacitor or inductor averages zero.
I use it all the time to check resistor wattage, regulator heat like (V in minus V out) times I for an LDO, and battery life."
